text: Every coding agent starts from zero. A teammate's agent worked on this code last week, and yours reads the same files all over again.
Finding the right file is the cheap part. More than nine tenths of the tokens go afterwards: the neighbouring code, the tests, the docs.
This is HandoffDB. It turns every finished agent run into a graph on HydraDB, so the next agent starts where the last one left off.
When a run ends, HandoffDB records what the agent opened and at which lines, the tests and docs it found, and where it decided the fix goes.
No model call. It just reads the run.
When the next task arrives, a few graph traversals go from its words to earlier runs, to the files they opened, to the tests they found.
Out comes a pack of about three hundred tokens.

Could a plain store do this? We built one from the same three hundred runs: a table from words to files. On a hundred later issues, the graph found every fix file and a real test about one time in three. The table, about one in five. Every setting was fixed in advance, on separate issues.
And it keeps learning. With no runs, it finds nothing. At twenty-five runs, about one in ten. At three hundred, one in three.
The usual handoff is a pile of notes. After three hundred runs, those notes come to about a hundred and fifty thousand tokens, and they keep growing. The pack stays at about three hundred.
Then we ran real agents. A fresh agent on an issue a teammate had already worked on: with the pack, success went from about seven in ten to more than eight in ten.
On brand-new issues, the pack costs no more than starting cold. Handing over the notes instead costs a third more.
Twenty agents asking at once, while new runs were being recorded: about a thousand packs in a minute, no errors, about a second each.
One agent learns. Every agent on the team starts there.
HandoffDB. Handoffs between coding agents, as a graph. Built on HydraDB.
